newsitem.title: USA: Calif. banker fined over campaign gifts -officials.
newsitem.headline: Calif. banker fined over campaign gifts -officials.

text.p: Calvin Grigsby, whose California firm is one of the largest African American-owned municipal bond underwriters in the United States, has paid a $5,000 fine for making campaign contributions without full and complete disclosure, state officials said on Monday.
Grigsby was not immediately available to comment.

The California Fair Political Practices Commission said Grigsby made campaign contributions totalling $11,500 in the first half of 1993. During the second half of 1993, Fiscal Funding Co Inc and other entities controlled by Grigsby made campaign contributions totaling $42,000.

The commission said Grigsby and Fiscal Funding failed to file timely major donor campaign statements reporting these contributions. Grigsby is a 50 percent owner and controlling partner of Fiscal Funding, an equipment leasing company.

In addition, the commission said Grigsby loaned money in December 1993 to Regina Bryant-Fields, who in turn contributed $4,500 to Alameda County Supervisor Mary King, who was then an Oakland, Calif., mayoral candidate.
"Grigsby knew or had reason to know that this loan would be used for the contribution to King, but neither Grigsby nor Bryant-Fields told King about the loan," the commission said.
Both Grigsby and Bryant-Fields maintain that they always intended the loan to be repaid. In April 1995, the loan was repaid in full to Grigsby.

But the commission said making a campaign contribution without full and complete disclosure that the contribution was funded by a loan from a third party "undermines the campaign disclosure provisions of the Political Reform Act and it deprives the electorate of essential information about who is supporting a candidate."
Grigsby has already paid the $5,000 fine, the commission said.
The commission said it could not comment on whether or not federal agencies were investigating the contributions.

"There may possibly be some violations of SEC rules," said commission Chair Ravi Mehta, referring to rules issued by the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board, whose activities are overseen by the Securities and Exchange Commission.
These rules limit the ability of municipal bond dealers to make political contributions to candidates in localities with which they do business.
"It's up to the SEC to deterimine whether any violations exist and whether any actions should be taken," Mehta said.
Grigsby's firm, Grigsby Brandford & Co of San Francisco, has handled several municipal bond underwritings in Alameda County, the state commission said.

"For that reason, there would have been additional public interest in learning information about contributions made by the respondents to members of the Alameda County Board of Supervisors," the commission said.
The California Fair Political Practices Commission enforces state rules that deal with political contributions and conflicts of interest.
